summary: Caisson lighthouse off Newport News, lit in 1891: keepers to 1954, rescues in the Lighthouse Service Bulletins, a 1937 death on station and a 2005 government auction.

structures.note: Tower of cast iron (USLHS). Caisson: 'iron' in the 1887 report and 'CAST IRON/CONCRETE CAISSON' in the USLHS record; 'the wooden caisson' in LighthouseFriends' 1890 account; concrete-filled per LighthouseFriends. Heights disagree: LighthouseFriends gives a 29 ft superstructure on a 56 ft caisson; USLHS gives 52 ft.

access.note: Privately owned since the 2005 government auction. The tower is closed; the owner must allow Coast Guard access for the beacon. Best viewed from the water or from the Interstate 664 bridge.

events.note: Work begins in spring; caisson towed to the site and sunk in July
Superstructure completed January 1891; formally accepted 6 March 1891
First exhibited from the lens on 15 April 1891
Assistant keeper Carl G. Marsh brings five people from a disabled motor boat (29 August)
Keeper M. D. Swain towed a disabled supply boat to the station (18 January)
Keeper Swain and assistant Tolson help three occupants of a motor boat lost in fog to reach a harbor (1 October; the entry prints no year; 1920 is the issue year)
Keeper H. T. (Homer T.) Austin helps occupants of a motor boat that ran into the station ladder in a storm (15 May; the Bulletin's OCR garbles the name, matched by LighthouseFriends and the roster)
Experiment: station roof marked with serial number for an airway in Chesapeake Bay (seaplanes)
Assistant keeper James B. Cox dies on station, 19 December 1937; coroner: acute coronary occlusion
Automated; characteristic changed to a white flash every six seconds
Decking torn away by an errant ship
Solar power installed; light moved to a pole above the gallery
Coast Guard spends $14,400 on sandblasting, painting, railings and a new access ladder
Offered under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act; no eligible agency or non-profit takes it
Sold at an online government-property auction for $31,000
A private family officially opens it as a residence on 4 July

notes_for_editor: Roster matched by name and position (0.03 km) and cited to the place page; the 52 spans are quoted as printed ('at least' and '-1954' kept). Charles Berry (1900-1901) appears only in LighthouseFriends and is included with that cite; no archive person. Mumford Guynn in LighthouseFriends is Mumford Gwynn in the story's source: the USLHS spelling (Guynn) is kept. LighthouseFriends says James B. Cox was transferred here in 1931; the USLHS roster lists him only from 1937. The story follows the roster and does not use the 1931 date. The 1920 Bulletin entry (October 1, three occupants of a motor boat lost in fog) prints no year; the entry sits among items dated late 1919, but the year is left unknown in the story; the event year 1920 is the issue year. The 1921 Bulletin's keeper name is OCR-broken ('H . T, Au still'); H. T. (Homer T.) Austin is matched by LighthouseFriends, the USLHS roster and the 1918-1923 Bulletin index ('Austin, H.T., keeper Newport News Middle Ground, assists motor boat'). The 1926 Bulletin's list line is OCR-garbled ('Newpo.rt :'Iews Middle Ground'); the reading Newport News Middle Ground is confirmed by the 1924-1929 index ('Newport News Middle Ground used in aerial navigation 135'). The 1919 Bulletin entry runs across printed pp. 67-68 (PDF p. 11). The 1914 Bulletin lists a 'Newport News, Va.' station among stations proposed for submarine groynes; the text does not say Middle Ground, so it is not used. The 1915-1922 Commissioner report mentions a 1921 motor-boat assistance by H. T. Austin and a commendations table naming Swain and Tolson; the table is OCR-split and was not used. Caisson material: the 1887 report asks for an iron caisson 35 ft in diameter; LighthouseFriends' 1890 account says 'the wooden caisson'; the USLHS record says 'CAST IRON/CONCRETE CAISSON'. The story states the disagreement. Not reconciled. Caisson diameter: 35 ft (1887 report, as requested) against 25 ft (LighthouseFriends, modern). Not reconciled; not used in the story. Height: LighthouseFriends gives a 29 ft superstructure on a 56 ft caisson; the USLHS record gives 52 ft height of light above mean high water and 52 ft base-to-lantern. Not reconciled; the story gives no tower height. Focal plane: LighthouseFriends 54 ft (the record's facts use 16.5 m from it); USLHS 52 ft above mean high water. Not reconciled; the story gives both. The record's characteristic (Fl R 10 s) is not confirmed by any source read; LighthouseFriends gives a white flash every six seconds from 1954, which the facts use. The current owner is a private individual, and LighthouseFriends names him with his family; the story does not name the owner or the family. LighthouseFriends names the temporary substitute keeper on 19 December 1937 (Wash Brown); the story leaves him unnamed. The NRHP nomination PDF (02001438) is a 'not yet digitised' placeholder; it was not read and is not cited. The 2002 NRHP offering in the record is not checked against the register; the story cites LighthouseFriends for the 2002 offer. A newspapers.py search was not run for this station; the story relies on LighthouseFriends and the Bulletin.
